title: Showing things with print
idea: A program is a list of instructions that Python follows from the top, one line at a time.
The instruction `print` shows something on the screen. Whatever you put inside the round brackets is what appears.
Words must sit inside quote marks. Quote marks tell Python: this is text, not an instruction. Numbers do not need quote marks.

title: Variables: names that hold values
idea: A variable is a name that holds a value, like a labelled box. You choose the name.
The single equals sign `=` means store. Python works out the right side first, then puts the answer in the name on the left.
You can change what a name holds later. The old value is thrown away.

title: One equals sign or two
idea: `=` stores a value. `==` asks a question: are these two things equal. The answer is `True` or `False`.
Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes. Say it aloud: one equals means put it in, two equals means is it the same.
`!=` asks the opposite question: are these different. `<` means less than and `>` means greater than.

title: The remainder with %
idea: The symbol `%` gives the remainder after dividing. 7 % 3 is 1, because 3 goes into 7 two times (that is 6) and 1 is left over.
If a number divides exactly, the remainder is 0. So `n % 2 == 0` is the standard way to ask: is n even.

title: Making choices with if and else
idea: An `if` line asks a yes or no question. If the answer is True, Python runs the indented lines under it. If False, it skips them.
`else` is the plan B. It runs only when the `if` question was False. `elif` means else if: another question, asked only when the earlier ones were False.
The colon `:` at the end of the line and the indent (4 spaces) are required. The indent shows which lines belong to the choice.

Each value sits in its own box, and each box has a number called its position (also called its index). The first box is position 0, not 1.
`append` adds a new value to the end of the list.

idea: To get one value out of a list, write the list name and the position in square brackets: `nums[0]` is the first value.
Positions start at 0. A list with 4 items has positions 0, 1, 2, 3. There is no position 4.
Negative positions count from the end. `nums[-1]` is the last item and `nums[-2]` is the one before it.
Asking for a position that does not exist stops the program with an IndexError.

title: Slicing: copying a piece of a list
idea: A slice copies a piece. Write `nums[a:b]`. It starts at position a and stops just before position b. The position b itself is not included.
A handy fact: `nums[a:b]` has exactly b - a items.
Leave a side empty to mean the edge: `nums[:3]` starts at the very beginning and `nums[2:]` goes to the very end. `nums[::-1]` is a reversed copy.

title: len and the last position
idea: `len(nums)` counts how many items are in the list. A list of 4 items has a length of 4.
Because positions start at 0, the last position is always `len(nums) - 1`. This is the heart of off-by-one mistakes: the length and the last position are different numbers.
Remember: for 4 items, length is 4, positions are 0 to 3, and the last position is 3.

title: range: counting numbers
idea: `range(n)` makes the numbers 0, 1, 2 and so on up to n - 1. It stops just before n, so it gives exactly n numbers.
`range(a, b)` starts at a and stops just before b. `range(a, b, step)` jumps by step each time.
Same rule as slicing: the end number is never included. To see the numbers, wrap it in `list( )`.

title: for loops: values versus positions
idea: A `for` loop repeats the indented lines. The name after `for` takes the next thing each time around.

There are two common shapes. Shape one, over values: `for x in nums:` gives you each item itself. Shape two, over positions: `for i in range(len(nums)):` gives you 0, 1, 2 and so on, and you write `nums[i]` to get the item.
Use shape one when you only need the items. Use shape two when you need to know where you are, or to look at neighbours like `nums[i + 1]`.

title: Functions and return
idea: A function is a named set of steps you can use again. You make one with `def`. The names in brackets are the inputs it receives, called parameters.
`return` sends an answer back to whoever used the function, and stops the function right there.
Printing and returning are different. Print shows something on the screen. Return hands a value back so other code can use it. HackerRank functions almost always return.

use the function, giving it 3 and 4

title: Reading input the HackerRank way
idea: On HackerRank, the test data does not live in your code. It arrives as typed lines. `input()` reads one line, always as text.

To turn text into a whole number use `int( )`. To read a line like `3 1 4` as a list of numbers, use `list(map(int, input().split()))`. Read it in pieces: `input()` gets the line, `.split()` cuts it at spaces into separate pieces of text, `int` turns each piece into a number, and `list` collects them.
The first line often tells you how many items follow. You usually read that line and then read the next one.

title: Strings: text is a row of letters
idea: Text in Python is called a string. A string works like a list of letters: it has positions starting at 0, and you can index and slice it the same way.
`len(word)` counts the letters. `word[0]` is the first letter. `word[::-1]` is the word reversed.

Useful tools: `.upper()` makes capitals, `.lower()` makes small letters, and `in` asks whether one piece of text is inside another. You cannot change a letter in place, you build a new string instead.

title: Dictionaries: looking things up by name
idea: A list finds an item by its position. A dictionary finds an item by a label that you choose, called a key. Think of a phone book: you look up a name (the key) and get a number (the value).
A dictionary is written with curly brackets. Each entry is a key, a colon, then a value: `ages = {"ana": 31, "bo": 27}`. Here "ana" is a key and 31 is its value.
`ages["ana"]` gives 31. Asking for a key that is not there stops the program with a KeyError. `ages.get("zed", 0)` gives 0 instead of stopping, because the second value is a fallback.
`ages["cy"] = 40` adds a new entry, or replaces the old value if the key already exists. `"ana" in ages` asks whether the key exists and answers True or False.
Counting is the most common use. For each item, add one to its count. The first time you meet an item it has no count yet, so `counts.get(item, 0) + 1` starts it at 0 and adds one.
`for key in counts:` visits each key in turn, and `counts[key]` gives its value. `sorted(counts)` gives the keys in order, which is useful when a question wants a stable answer.
Why bother: Python finds a key almost instantly however big the dictionary is. Looking for a value inside a list means checking items one by one. A dictionary lets you avoid a loop inside a loop.
symbols: separates a key from its value
the value under key, or the fallback when the key is missing

title: Sorting: putting items in order
idea: `sorted(items)` gives a new list in order: smallest to largest for numbers, A to Z for text. The original list is left as it was.
`items.sort()` puts the list itself in order and gives back nothing (the value None). So `x = items.sort()` leaves x empty. This is a very common mistake.
`sorted(items, reverse=True)` goes from largest to smallest.

`key=` tells sorted what to look at when it compares two items. A key function takes one item and returns the value to compare. `sorted(words, key=len)` puts shorter words first, because `len` gives each word's length.
A key can return a pair such as `(len(w), w)`. Python compares the first value, and only looks at the second when the first values are equal. That is how you break ties.
`lambda w: (len(w), w)` is a tiny function with no name. Read it as: given w, hand back the pair (len(w), w). Writing `-score` in a key flips the order for that part, so biggest comes first.
Sorting makes many problems easy. After sorting, the closest values sit next to each other, and equal values sit side by side.
symbols: a new list with the items of x in order
puts x itself in order, returns None
a tiny function: given w, hand back the value after the colon
a pair, compared first part first

example.caption: sorted gives a new list and leaves nums alone. The last line orders words by length.
example.code:
nums = [5, 2, 9, 1]
ordered = sorted(nums)
print(nums)
print(ordered)
words = ["pear", "fig", "apple"]
by_size = sorted(words, key=len)
print(by_size)

title: Two pointers: walking in from both ends
idea: A pointer is just a variable that holds a position. Two pointers means two such variables, usually called `left` and `right`.
The most common set-up: `left` starts at position 0, `right` starts at the last position, which is `len(nums) - 1`. Then you move them toward each other.
Use `while left < right:` to keep going until they meet. Inside, decide which pointer moves. `left += 1` means add 1 to left. `right -= 1` means take 1 away from right.
Always move at least one pointer every round. If neither moves, the loop never ends and the program times out.
Why it helps: checking every pair of items needs a loop inside a loop. With two pointers on a sorted list, each step safely rules something out, so one pass is enough.
A second style has both pointers start at the left. A slow pointer marks where the next good value goes, and a fast pointer scans ahead. Problems about removing duplicates use that style.
Shaky spot to watch: `left < right` stops when they meet. `left <= right` would also test the single middle item. For mirrored pairs, `<` is usually right.
symbols: repeat while left is still before right

visuals.title: Pointers start at the two ends and walk inward.

example.caption: Reverse a row of letters by swapping the two ends and moving inward. Watch left and right walk toward each other.
example.code:
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
left = 0
right = len(letters) - 1
while left < right:
    temp = letters[left]
    letters[left] = letters[right]
    letters[right] = temp
    left += 1
    right -= 1
print(letters)

        left += 1
    else:
        right -= 1
print(found)

title: Sliding window: a block of neighbours
idea: A window is a block of neighbouring items, for example positions 2, 3 and 4. A sliding window moves along the list one step at a time.

The trick is to not start again from scratch. When the window moves one step right, one new item comes in on the right and one old item drops out on the left. Update the total by adding the new item and taking away the old one.
That turns a loop inside a loop (add up every block separately) into one pass. For a list of 100000 numbers, that is the difference between finishing and timing out.

Fixed size: the window always holds k items. Start by adding the first k, then slide. Variable size: grow the window by moving `right`, and shrink it by moving `left` while a rule is broken or a goal is met.
The size of a window from `left` to `right`, with both ends included, is `right - left + 1`. Draw it with two items to check: left 3 and right 4 is 2 items, and 4 - 3 + 1 is 2.
Shaky spot to watch: off-by-one. A window of k items that ends at position `right` starts at `right - k + 1`, not `right - k`.
In the pictures, the green boxes are the current window.
symbols: the total (or count) of the items currently inside the block
position of the first item in the window
position of the last item in the window
how many items are in the window

visuals.title: A window of 3 items from left=1 to right=3

example.caption: Best total of 3 neighbours. Each step adds the item that enters on the right and takes away the one that leaves on the left. Green boxes are the window.
example.code:
nums = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
left = 0
right = 2
window = nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2]
best = window
while right < len(nums) - 1:
    right += 1
    window = window + nums[right] - nums[left]
    left += 1
    if window > best:
        best = window
print(best)

example2.caption: Shortest block with a total of at least 7. Move right to grow the window. While the total is big enough, record the size and shrink from the left. Here 99 means no answer yet.

target = 7
left = 0
total = 0
best = 99
for right in range(len(nums)):
    total += nums[right]
    while total >= target:
        size = right - left + 1
        if size < best:
            best = size
        total -= nums[left]
        left += 1
print(best)

title: 2D grids: rows and columns
idea: A grid is a list of lists. Each inner list is one row. `grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]` has 2 rows and 3 columns.
To pick one cell write two positions: `grid[r][c]`. The first one, `r`, is the row (counting down from 0). The second one, `c`, is the column (counting across from 0). `grid[1][2]` is 6.

The number of rows is `len(grid)`. The number of columns is `len(grid[0])`, the length of the first row. These are different numbers unless the grid is square. Mixing them up is the classic grid mistake.
To visit every cell use a loop inside a loop: `for r in range(len(grid)):` then `for c in range(len(grid[0])):`.

Neighbours: the cell above is row `r - 1`, below is `r + 1`, left is column `c - 1`, right is `c + 1`. A list of four changes does the work: `for dr, dc in [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]:`. Here dr means change in row and dc means change in column.

Before reading a neighbour, check that it is on the grid: `0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols`. Without it, you get an IndexError at the edges, or worse, a negative position quietly wraps around to the far side.
In the pictures the yellow cell is the one at row `r`, column `c`.
symbols: the cell in row r, column c
change in row, change in column
nr is on the grid (a chained comparison)
row and column of the neighbour

visuals.title: grid[1][2] is the yellow cell, which holds 6

example.caption: Add up every cell. The outer loop picks a row, the inner loop walks across it. The yellow cell shows where r and c are.

example2.caption: Add up the four neighbours of the middle cell. The check on nr and nc keeps us on the grid.
example2.code:
grid = [[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 0]]
r = 1
c = 1
count = 0
for dr, dc in [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]:
    nr = r + dr
    nc = c + dc
    if 0 <= nr < 3 and 0 <= nc < 3:
        count += grid[nr][nc]
print(count)

title: Text tools: split, join, replace and friends
idea: Text (a string) is a row of characters. It has built-in tools called methods. You write the text, a dot, the tool name and brackets: `line.split()`.
Text cannot be changed in place. Every tool gives back new text and leaves the original alone, so keep the result: `clean = line.strip()`.
`split()` cuts text into a list of words at the spaces. `split(",")` cuts at commas instead. `" ".join(words)` does the reverse: it glues a list of words together with a space between each.
`strip()` removes spaces from both ends. `lower()` and `upper()` change the case. `replace("cat", "dog")` swaps every `cat` for `dog`.
`"big" in line` is True when `big` appears anywhere inside line. `line.startswith("ab")` is True when line begins with ab.
A very handy pair: `" ".join(line.split())` squeezes any run of spaces down to a single space and removes spaces at the ends.
symbols: cut s into a list of words
glue words together with a space
True when a appears in s

visuals.title: "hi you".split() gives a list of two words

example.code:
line = "  Hello   Big World "
words = line.split()
print(words)
print(" ".join(words).lower())
print("big" in line.lower())

text = "the cat and the hat"
print(text.replace("the", "a"))
print(text.upper())
print(text.startswith("the"))

title: Parsing: turning text lines into data
idea: Parsing means reading a line of text and pulling out the pieces you need. Input always arrives as text, even when it looks like a number.
The usual recipe is split, then convert. `parts = "ana,31,rome".split(",")` gives `['ana', '31', 'rome']`. Then `int(parts[1])` turns the text `31` into the number 31.
If you forget `int(...)`, the plus sign glues text instead of adding: `"4" + "10"` is `410`, not 14. Text numbers also sort wrongly, because `"10"` comes before `"9"` letter by letter.
When a line always has exactly two pieces, you can name them in one go: `name, amount = line.split()`. If there are not exactly two pieces, Python stops with a ValueError.
Many lines arrive as a count followed by that many lines. Read them with `lines = [input() for _ in range(n)]`. The `_` is just a name for a variable you do not need.
Records often combine two ideas from earlier: parse each line, then store the pieces in a dictionary, for example to add up amounts per name.
symbols: cut line at the commas into a list
turn text such as "31" into the number 31
name the two pieces in one step
read n lines into a list
turn the number n into text

example.caption: Split a record, then turn the age into a number so we can add to it.
example.code:
record = "ana,31,rome"
parts = record.split(",")
name = parts[0]
age = int(parts[1])
city = parts[2]
print(name, age + 1, city)

title: Characters: checking and shifting letters
idea: Looping over text with `for ch in s:` visits one character at a time. Each character is itself a piece of text of length 1.
Character tests give True or False: `ch.isdigit()` for 0 to 9, `ch.isalpha()` for letters, `ch.isupper()` and `ch.islower()` for case.
Every character has a number code. `ord(ch)` gives the number, and `chr(number)` gives the character back. The lowercase letters a to z have codes 97 to 122 in order.
So `ord(ch) - ord("a")` is the place of a letter in the alphabet, counting a as 0 and z as 25.
To wrap around the end of the alphabet use the remainder: `(place + shift) % 26`. After z comes a again. This uses the % idea from earlier.
To build new text, start with an empty text `result = ""` and glue characters on with `result += ch`. Remember that text numbers need `str(...)` before you glue them.
symbols: True when ch is a digit
remainder after dividing by 26, which wraps around
glue ch onto the end of result

title: Big O: how fast does the work grow
idea: Big O is a way to talk about how the amount of work grows as the input gets bigger. We count steps, not seconds, because seconds depend on the computer.
Call the size of the input `n`, for example the number of items in a list. If one loop visits every item once, the work is about n steps. We say that is O(n), read as order n or linear.
A loop inside a loop, where both go over n items, does about n times n steps. That is O(n squared), written O(n^2). With n = 100000 that is ten billion steps, far too slow for a test.

O(1), constant, means the work does not grow with n. Looking up a dictionary key or reading `nums[3]` is O(1). O(log n) means the work grows very slowly because each step halves the problem. Sorting is O(n log n).
Drop small parts. A solution that takes 2n + 5 steps is still O(n). A solution with n squared plus n steps is O(n squared), because the biggest part wins.

Rules of thumb for Python: one loop is O(n). A loop inside a loop is O(n^2). `x in a_list` is O(n) because it may check every item. `x in a_dict` or `x in a_set` is O(1). `sorted(items)` is O(n log n).
Space means extra memory. A new list or dictionary that grows with n costs O(n) space. Many answers trade extra space for speed: storing items in a dictionary uses memory but removes a loop.
symbols: constant: work does not grow with n
grows very slowly: the problem is halved each step
linear: work grows in step with n
a little more than linear, for example sorting
quadratic: a loop inside a loop
